newsitem.title: USA: NYS lawmakers unveil $2.4 bln plan to boost revs.
newsitem.headline: NYS lawmakers unveil $2.4 bln plan to boost revs.

text.p: A group of Democratic New York State lawmakers Tuesday unveiled what they called a "tax fairness" plan to raise $2.4 billion of revenues by increasing taxes on the wealthy and closing corporate tax loopholes.
The Democrats argued that a series of income tax reductions by Gov George Patki had hurt New Yorkers because they were paid for with big spending cuts and increases in college tuition and other fees.

Saying the Republican governor's tax-cutting program had shifted the tax burden to the middle-class from the wealthy, New York State Senator Franz Leichter (D-Manhattan), in prepared remarks, said: "Local property tax and user fee increases far exceed the savings low and middle income working New Yorkers have received from the Pataki tax cuts."
A spokesman for the state budget office was not immediately available to comment on the lawmakers' proposal.
Leichter also faulted Pataki for failing to create jobs, saying fewer jobs new jobs have been created uner Pataki's first two years in office than in former Governor Mario Cuomo's last two years.

In December, the state unemployment rate stood at 5.8 percent, according to the New York State Department of Labor. While this rate was one percentage point above the rate in November, the latest reading was at its lowest level in December since 1990.

The new bill, which was backed by 36 out of the 96 Democratic members of the Assembly and eight of 26 of the Democratic Senators, along with nine unions and 81 advocacy groups, would repeal the final year of the personal income tax cut for joint filers who make more than $100,000.
This step that would prevent New York State from losing $350 million of revenues in fiscal 1998, the lawmakers said.

Further, the measure would eliminate the investment tax credit and several other corporate tax loopholes, as well as negate a cut in the corporate tax surcharge, which went into effect in 1996. The lawmakers said this would raise about $750 million a year.

Finally, a one-percent surcharge, which would be dedicated to pay for school improvements, would be paid by joint filers with adjusted gross incomes of over $150,000 a year. A two-percent levy would be paid by joint filers whose gross incomes added up to over $200,000.
These two surcharges would raise about $1.3 billion a year, the lawmakers said.
